title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Background


The data

Spanish motor insurance portfolio
354,140 policies, 2022 to 2024
47 variables: policyholder, vehicle, premium, claims

Source: García-Pérez (2024), Mendeley Data

The business question
Which policy, driver and vehicle characteristics drive:

the portfolio’s profitability (Loss Ratio)?
the portfolio’s volatility (dispersion of Loss Ratio)?



This portfolio is loss-making on average and the underwriting team wants to understand why. We use visual analytics on the full 354,000-policy dataset to surface the variables most strongly associated with profitability and volatility. The headline outcome is Loss Ratio — incurred losses divided by premium — and we measure volatility through the coefficient of variation of Loss Ratio within risk segments.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Portfolio Snapshot


























The portfolio more than doubled between 2022 and 2024 — any YoY KPI movement must be read in light of this rapid mix shift.
New business accounts for ≈ 70% of policies each year — the book is in an aggressive acquisition phase, not a steady renewal state.
CC (third-party + add-ons) covers nearly 60% of policies; the basic TP tier is the smallest segment.





The portfolio more than doubled between 2022 and 2024 — any year-over-year movement in KPIs needs to be read in light of this rapid mix shift. New business accounts for about 70% of policies each year. On the product side, CC (third-party plus several add-ons) covers nearly 60% of the book, followed by COMP_E. The basic TP tier is the smallest segment.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
COMP_N: highest loss ratio


























COMP_N has a mean Loss Ratio of 0.82, roughly double the rest of the book and well above the break-even line of 1.0.
The distribution shape on the right shows COMP_N carries both a higher peak and a fatter right tail — more frequent moderate losses and more extreme outliers.
Repricing or restructuring this single product is the most direct lever available to underwriting; it covers ≈ 16,000 policies.





COMP_N — comprehensive cover without an excess — has a mean Loss Ratio of 0.82, roughly double the rest of the book. The ridge plot on the right shows the reason: COMP_N has both a higher peak and a fatter right tail, meaning more frequent moderate losses and more extreme outliers. Repricing or restructuring this single product is the most direct lever the underwriting team has on profitability.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Bonus score predicts claim frequency


























Bad-bonus drivers file 0.71 claims per policy-year versus 0.31 for Good — a 2.3× gap.
22% of Bad-bonus policies had at least one claim, vs 14% for Good — chi-square test confirms p < 0.001.
The bonus-malus system therefore mainly captures frequency risk; the bigger the bonus discount, the rarer the claim filing.





The Spanish bonus-malus system works as intended. Bad-bonus drivers report 0.71 claims per policy-year versus 0.31 for Good-bonus drivers — a 2.3× gap that a chi-square test confirms is highly significant. The right chart shows the same pattern from a different angle: 22% of Bad-bonus policies had at least one claim, against 14% for Good. The bonus score therefore captures frequency risk far more strongly than severity risk.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Bonus does not predict severity


























Claim severity distributions overlap almost perfectly across the three bonus groups — same median (≈ EUR 500), same shape.
Bad-bonus drivers claim 2.3× more often (frequency) but each claim is only 1.19× more expensive (severity).
Pricing models that already include the bonus discount do not need additional severity loading for Bad-bonus drivers.





The violin plot on the left shows that the distribution of claim severity is nearly identical across bonus groups — same shape, same median (around EUR 500). The bar chart on the right makes the contrast explicit: Bad-bonus drivers file claims 2.3 times more often than Good, but each individual claim is only 1.19 times more expensive on average. This is an important pricing insight. The bonus-malus system effectively prices risky drivers by predicting how often they will crash, not how severely. Pricing models that already include the bonus discount do not need additional severity loading for Bad-bonus drivers.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Driver age: U-shape


























Loss Ratio peaks at age extremes (≤25 and ≥65) and bottoms out in the 36–50 band — the classic motor underwriting U-shape.
The U-shape repeats within every bonus group, but the gap between Bad and Good widens at the extremes.
The worst sub-segment in the entire portfolio is young drivers (≤25) carrying a Bad bonus score.





Loss Ratio peaks at the two age extremes — drivers aged 25 and under and drivers aged 65 and over — and bottoms out in the 36-50 band. This is the classic U-shape that motor underwriters expect. The right panel shows the U-shape repeats inside every bonus group, but the gap widens at the extremes. Young Bad-bonus drivers are by far the most loss-making sub-segment in the portfolio.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Profit ≠ Stability


























TP has the lowest mean Loss Ratio (0.31) but the highest CV (5.19) — profitable on average yet exposed to severe spikes.
The Good-bonus group is the most profitable yet has the highest CV — low losses are usually small, but rare large losses still occur.
Profitability and volatility must be managed as two separate KPIs; tracking only the mean hides accumulating tail risk.





The most profitable segments are not always the most stable. TP — the cheapest third-party tier — has the lowest mean Loss Ratio but the highest coefficient of variation because a small number of severe liability claims swing the segment. Similarly, the Good-bonus group has the highest CV despite being the most profitable on average. Profitability and volatility therefore need separate management — pricing alone is not enough.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Tail risk: concentrated, not random


























The heatmap shows Bad-bonus policies are 2× more likely to fall into the highest loss-ratio bands (>1) than Good-bonus policies.
Among loss-bearing policies, COMP_N has the largest share with Loss Ratio above 2 — paying out more than twice the premium collected.
Tail risk is not random — it concentrates exactly where the mean Loss Ratio is also highest.





The heatmap on the left shows that Bad-bonus policyholders are roughly twice as likely as Good-bonus ones to fall into the most loss-making bands above LR > 1. The right chart isolates the tail: among loss-bearing policies, COMP_N has the highest share with Loss Ratio above 2 — the policies that pay out more than twice the premium collected. Tail risk is therefore concentrated where mean Loss Ratio is also highest.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Trend: profitability is deteriorating


























Overall Loss Ratio rose 22% in two years (0.38 → 0.46); COMP_N crossed the break-even line in 2024 (LR = 1.01).
Renewals consistently underperform new business by 5–8 percentage points — the gap is widening, not narrowing.
This is adverse selection in retention: the better customers shop around, the riskier ones stay.





Three independent signals point to the same conclusion. The left chart shows COMP_N has crossed break-even in 2024 — every euro collected is now paid out in claims. The right chart reveals an even more concerning pattern: renewals consistently underperform new business, and the gap is widening. This is the classic adverse selection problem in insurance — the good customers shop around at renewal time and find cheaper quotes elsewhere, while the riskier customers, who would struggle to find a better deal, stay. The portfolio’s risk profile is deteriorating faster than the underwriting team is responding.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Geography and fuel: small effects


























Geographic (municipality, urban/rural) and fuel-type splits produce <0.12 of Loss Ratio difference — statistically significant but practically small.
Compared to the 0.51 spread driven by policy type and 0.16 by driver age, these are second-order effects.
Pricing effort should concentrate on the top three dimensions: policy type, bonus score, and driver age.





Geography and fuel type are statistically significant — with 354,000 observations almost everything is — but the magnitudes are small. Rural beats Urban by 0.07 of Loss Ratio, and Diesel exceeds Gasoline by 0.11. Compared to the 0.51 spread driven by policy type or the 0.16 U-shape across driver age, these are second-order effects. The right chart ranks all six dimensions by the size of the spread they produce; the bottom three are too small to justify their own pricing factor. Pricing effort should concentrate on the top three dimensions: policy type, bonus, and driver age.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Business Impacts: Pricing & Product


Re-price or restructure COMP_N

Mean LR = 0.82, crossed break-even in 2024
Highest tail share (LR > 2)
≈ 16,000 policies — meaningful portfolio impact

Address renewal adverse selection

Renewals 8pp worse than new business and widening
Risk-segment retention: protect good renewals, let worst ones lapse
Avoid across-the-board renewal discounts


Apply differentiated underwriting to drivers ≤ 25 with Bad bonus

Worst sub-segment (age extreme × frequency risk)
Tighter UW rules, mandatory excess, or selective non-renewal

Re-examine TP pricing & reinsurance

Mean LR low (0.31) but highest CV (5.19)
Exposed to severe liability claims
Review excess-of-loss reinsurance structures



These are the four highest-leverage actions. Re-pricing COMP_N to the portfolio average would lift overall Loss Ratio by 1.5 to 2.0 percentage points on its own. The young Bad-bonus underwriting tightening adds roughly another point. The renewal adverse selection point is the newest finding from the temporal analysis — it suggests the retention team and the underwriting team need to coordinate on which renewals to protect versus which to let go. Combined, these actions could improve underwriting result by 3 to 4 percentage points of Loss Ratio.

title: Profitability and Volatility
text:
Business Impacts: Portfolio Management


Track profitability and volatility separately

Most profitable segments are not the most stable
Mean LR alone hides tail risk
Add CV / tail share to standard reporting

Adjust for new-business mix

≈ 70% of policies are new each year
Headline trends confounded by mix shift
Use stratified or mix-adjusted KPIs


Focus monitoring on 5 risk cells

COMP_N policies (all)
Drivers ≤ 25 with Bad bonus
Drivers ≥ 65 (all bonus levels)
TP policies (volatility watch)
Policies with prior-year LR > 2

These cells capture most of the portfolio’s downside.


On the portfolio management side, the main shift is conceptual: profitability and volatility must be managed as two separate dimensions. The five risk cells listed on the right give the underwriting committee a focused watchlist instead of monitoring dozens of metrics across all dimensions. The mix-adjustment point matters because the book is in an aggressive growth phase — headline KPI movements would otherwise be confounded by changing new-business share.

3.4 Cleaning and Converting Variables

#Dropping zero-exposure records and converting categorical variables to factors
clean <- raw %>%
  filter(!(total_premium == 0 & total_exposure == 0)) %>%
  mutate(
    policy_type = factor(policy_type,
                         levels = c("TP", "TPG", "CC", "COMP_E", "COMP_N")),
    policy_status = factor(policy_status, levels = c("A", "C"),
                           labels = c("Active", "Cancelled")),
    business_type = factor(business_type, levels = c("NB", "P"),
                           labels = c("New business", "Portfolio")),
    fuel_type = factor(fuel_type, levels = c("D", "G"),
                       labels = c("Diesel", "Gasoline")),
    municipality_type = factor(municipality_type, levels = c("I", "C", "IS"),
                               labels = c("Inland", "Coastal", "Islands")),
    circulation_area = factor(circulation_area, levels = c("U", "R"),
                              labels = c("Urban", "Rural")),
    payment_frequency = factor(payment_frequency, 
                               levels = c("A", "S", "Q"),
                               labels = c("Annual", "Semi-annual", "Quarterly"),
                               ordered = TRUE),
    bonus_score = factor(bonus_score, levels = c("B", "N", "G"),
                         labels = c("Bad", "Neutral", "Good"),
                         ordered = TRUE),
    year_fct = factor(year),
    vehicle_brand = fct_lump_n(vehicle_brand, n = 15, other_level = "Other")
  )

bonus_score and payment_frequency are treated as ordered factors. vehicle_brand originally has 68 unique values with a long tail; the top 15 are kept and the rest grouped as “Other”.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
3.5 Creating Profitability and Volatility KPIs

#Building analytical KPIs with division-by-zero guards
clean <- clean %>%
  mutate(
    loss_ratio = if_else(total_premium > 0,
                         total_incurred / total_premium, NA_real_),
    frequency = if_else(total_exposure > 0,
                        total_claims / total_exposure, NA_real_),
    severity = if_else(total_claims > 0,
                       total_incurred / total_claims, NA_real_),
    pure_premium = if_else(total_exposure > 0,
                           total_incurred / total_exposure, NA_real_),
    has_claim = total_claims > 0
  )

Four KPIs are derived:

loss_ratio = incurred ÷ premium — the headline profitability indicator
frequency = claims ÷ exposure — expected number of claims per policy-year
severity = incurred ÷ claims — average cost per claim
pure_premium = incurred ÷ exposure ≈ Frequency × Severity

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
4.2 Statistical Validation Strategy
Because the sample size is large (≈ 354,000 policies), conventional p-value cutoffs lose their discriminating power — almost every difference is “significant”. Three deliberate adjustments are therefore applied throughout the bivariate analysis:

Non-parametric tests by default. Loss Ratio is heavily right-skewed and zero-inflated, violating the normality assumption behind ANOVA and Pearson correlation. Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney and Spearman are used instead.
Effect size, not just p-value. Each interpretation paragraph reports the actual magnitude of the difference (e.g. “0.82 vs 0.41”) rather than relying on significance alone.
Winsorisation at the 99th percentile. Extreme Loss Ratio values (the maximum is 11,349) would distort group means and plot scales. Winsorising at the 99th percentile preserves all observations while preventing tail outliers from dominating visual and statistical comparisons.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
4.3 Why ggstatsplot
Most bivariate plots in this report use ggstatsplot instead of plain ggplot2. The reason is that this package embeds the statistical test result inside the plot itself — sample size, test statistic, p-value, effect size, and pairwise comparisons all appear in the figure caption automatically. This satisfies the assignment’s requirement for “statistically validated” findings without forcing readers to flip between charts and a separate results table.

text:
5.1 Numerical Variables

5.1.1 Driver Age

#Plotting driver age distribution with a histogram
ggplot(clean, aes(x = driver_age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#7097BB", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Driver Age",
       x = "Driver age (years)", y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_minimal()








Driver age is roughly symmetric and centred around 48 years, ranging from 18 to 90. There is no extreme skew, and the bulk of the portfolio sits between 35 and 65.


5.1.2 Vehicle Age

#Plotting vehicle age distribution
ggplot(clean, aes(x = vehicle_age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#7097BB", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Vehicle Age",
       x = "Vehicle age (years)", y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_minimal()








Vehicle age is also fairly symmetric with a median of 25 years. The portfolio leans towards older vehicles, which is consistent with the typical Spanish private motor market.


5.1.3 Vehicle Value

#Plotting vehicle value on a log scale due to heavy right skew
ggplot(clean %>% filter(!is.na(vehicle_value)), aes(x = vehicle_value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#7097BB", color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Vehicle Value (log scale)",
       x = "Vehicle value (€, log scale)", y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_minimal()








Vehicle value is heavily right-skewed (skewness ≈ 2.2), so a log scale is used to reveal the shape. Most vehicles are valued between €10,000 and €40,000, with a long tail of luxury vehicles extending past €300,000.


5.1.4 Total Premium

#Plotting total premium distribution on a log scale
ggplot(clean, aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#7097BB", color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Premium (log scale)",
       x = "Total premium (€, log scale)", y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_minimal()








Total premium ranges from less than €1 to over €5,000 and is strongly right-skewed. On a log scale the distribution looks roughly bell-shaped, with most policies clustered between €150 and €500.


5.1.5 Total Incurred (Claims with losses only)

#Plotting incurred losses for policies that actually had claims
ggplot(clean %>% filter(total_incurred > 0), aes(x = total_incurred)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#D95F02", color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Incurred Losses (Loss-bearing policies only, log scale)",
       x = "Incurred amount (€, log scale)", y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_minimal()








Only 14.3% of policies had any incurred losses. Among those, the distribution is extremely right-skewed even on a log scale, with a small number of catastrophic claims exceeding €100,000. This long tail is the main source of portfolio volatility.


5.1.6 Loss Ratio

#Plotting loss ratio for loss-bearing policies, capped at 99th percentile
clean %>%
  filter(loss_ratio > 0) %>%
  filter(loss_ratio <= quantile(loss_ratio, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#D95F02", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Loss Ratio (Loss-bearing policies, capped at p99)",
       x = "Loss ratio (incurred / premium)", y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_minimal()








The dashed line at 1.0 marks the break-even point. Among loss-bearing policies, the median loss ratio is 2.3 — meaning the median loss-bearing policy paid out more than twice its premium. Tail values reach into the tens and hundreds, which strongly affects portfolio profitability.

5.2.4 Vehicle Brand (Top 15)

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
6.1 Drivers of Profitability

6.1.1 Bonus Score and Loss Ratio

#Comparing loss ratio across bonus score groups with Kruskal-Wallis test
ggbetweenstats(
  data = clean_sample %>% filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)),
  x = bonus_score,
  y = loss_ratio_w,
  type = "np",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  ylab = "Loss ratio (Winsorised at p99)"
)








Policyholders with a “Bad” bonus score have a mean Loss Ratio about 30% higher than those with “Good” — 0.56 vs 0.42. The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms the difference is significant, and the pairwise comparisons show that all three groups differ from each other. This validates the bonus-malus system: the historical claims record genuinely predicts future loss experience.


6.1.2 Policy Type and Loss Ratio

#Comparing loss ratio across policy types
ggbetweenstats(
  data = clean_sample %>% filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)),
  x = policy_type,
  y = loss_ratio_w,
  type = "np",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  ylab = "Loss ratio (Winsorised at p99)"
)








COMP_N (comprehensive without excess) has a mean Loss Ratio of 0.82 — roughly twice the level of the other policy types. This is the most important business finding so far: the broadest coverage tier is the least profitable. TP and TPG (third-party variants) are the most profitable on average, consistent with their narrower coverage.


6.1.3 Circulation Area and Loss Ratio

#Comparing urban vs rural with Mann-Whitney test
ggbetweenstats(
  data = clean_sample %>% filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)),
  x = circulation_area,
  y = loss_ratio_w,
  type = "np",
  ylab = "Loss ratio (Winsorised at p99)"
)








Urban policies have a mean Loss Ratio of 0.445 versus 0.409 for rural — a small but significant gap. The effect size is modest, suggesting that geography matters less than policy type or bonus score.


6.1.4 Driver Age and Loss Ratio

#Examining loss ratio across driver age bands
ggbetweenstats(
  data = clean_sample %>% filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w), !is.na(driver_age_band)),
  x = driver_age_band,
  y = loss_ratio_w,
  type = "np",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  ylab = "Loss ratio (Winsorised at p99)"
)








Loss Ratio is highest for the youngest drivers (≤25) and the oldest (65+), forming the classic U-shape known to motor underwriters. The middle-age bands (26–50) are the most profitable.


6.1.5 Fuel Type and Loss Ratio

#Comparing diesel vs gasoline
ggbetweenstats(
  data = clean_sample %>% filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w), !is.na(fuel_type)),
  x = fuel_type,
  y = loss_ratio_w,
  type = "np",
  ylab = "Loss ratio (Winsorised at p99)"
)








The gap between diesel and gasoline policies is statistically significant but very small in magnitude. Fuel type alone is unlikely to be a useful pricing factor.


6.1.6 Bonus Score and Claim Frequency

#Linking bonus score to claim frequency
ggbetweenstats(
  data = clean_sample %>% filter(!is.na(frequency)),
  x = bonus_score,
  y = frequency,
  type = "np",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  ylab = "Claim frequency (claims / exposure)"
)








The frequency gap is larger than the Loss Ratio gap: “Bad” bonus drivers file claims at 0.71 per policy-year versus 0.31 for “Good”. The bonus score therefore mainly captures frequency risk, not severity.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
6.2 Drivers of Volatility
Volatility is measured here as the coefficient of variation (CV) of Loss Ratio within each group — standard deviation divided by mean. A higher CV means more unpredictable losses for that segment, even if the average is not extreme.

6.2.1 Coefficient of Variation by Policy Type

#Computing CV of loss ratio by policy type
cv_policy <- clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)) %>%
  group_by(policy_type) %>%
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio_w),
            sd_lr = sd(loss_ratio_w),
            cv = sd_lr / mean_lr,
            n = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv))

ggplot(cv_policy, aes(x = fct_reorder(policy_type, cv), y = cv)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#D95F02") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(cv, 2)), hjust = -0.2, size = 4) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio Volatility by Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Coefficient of variation (higher = more unpredictable)",
       x = NULL, y = "Coefficient of variation") +
  theme_minimal()








TP (third-party only) is the most volatile despite having the lowest mean Loss Ratio. This is because the small number of severe third-party liability claims can cause large swings relative to the modest average. COMP_N is the least volatile in relative terms, partly because its mean is already high.


6.2.2 Ridge Plot of Loss Ratio by Policy Type

#Showing full distribution shapes side by side
clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w), loss_ratio_w > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio_w, y = policy_type, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_density_ridges(scale = 1.5, rel_min_height = 0.01, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Loss Ratio by Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Loss-bearing policies only, Winsorised at p99",
       x = "Loss ratio", y = NULL) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The ridge plot shows that COMP_N not only has the highest mean but also a fatter right tail — meaning extreme losses are more common in this segment. The other policy types have similar shapes but differ in where their tails extend.


6.2.3 Coefficient of Variation by Bonus Score

#CV of loss ratio by bonus score
cv_bonus <- clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)) %>%
  group_by(bonus_score) %>%
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio_w),
            sd_lr = sd(loss_ratio_w),
            cv = sd_lr / mean_lr,
            n = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv))

ggplot(cv_bonus, aes(x = bonus_score, y = cv)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#D95F02") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(cv, 2)), vjust = -0.3, size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio Volatility by Bonus Score",
       x = "Bonus score", y = "Coefficient of variation") +
  theme_minimal()








The “Good” bonus group has the highest relative volatility (CV ≈ 4.0) — even though its mean Loss Ratio is the lowest. This is a subtle but important finding: although Good-bonus policies are profitable on average, when losses do occur they can be relatively large compared to the low average, creating tail risk.


6.2.4 Loss Ratio Band × Bonus Score (Heatmap)

#Cross-tabulating loss ratio bands with bonus score
clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio)) %>%
  mutate(
    lr_band = case_when(
      loss_ratio == 0 ~ "0",
      loss_ratio <= 0.5 ~ "(0, 0.5]",
      loss_ratio <= 1 ~ "(0.5, 1]",
      loss_ratio <= 2 ~ "(1, 2]",
      TRUE ~ ">2"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("0", "(0, 0.5]", "(0.5, 1]", "(1, 2]", ">2"))
  ) %>%
  count(bonus_score, lr_band) %>%
  group_by(bonus_score) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lr_band, y = bonus_score, fill = share)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F0F4F8", high = "#1F4E79",
                      labels = label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio Band Share by Bonus Score",
       x = "Loss ratio band", y = "Bonus score", fill = "Share") +
  theme_minimal()








Reading across each row of the heatmap, “Bad” bonus policyholders are roughly twice as likely as “Good” ones to fall into the loss-making bands (>2 and (1, 2]). The bonus score is therefore a strong directional signal for both mean Loss Ratio and the share of policies in the tail.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
6.3 Multivariate Patterns

6.3.1 Has-Claim × Bonus Score (Stacked Bar with Chi-Square)

#Chi-square test between has-claim and bonus score
ggbarstats(
  data = clean_sample,
  x = has_claim,
  y = bonus_score,
  label = "percentage",
  legend.title = "Has claim"
)








The chi-square test confirms a strong association between bonus score and the probability of filing a claim. 22% of “Bad” bonus policies had at least one claim, versus 14% for “Good” — a 1.5× ratio. This is the cleanest single dimension separating risky from safe customers.


6.3.2 Loss Ratio by Driver Age Band and Bonus Score (Faceted)

#Loss ratio across two factors simultaneously
clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w), !is.na(driver_age_band)) %>%
  group_by(driver_age_band, bonus_score) %>%
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio_w), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = driver_age_band, y = mean_lr,
             group = bonus_score, color = bonus_score)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Bad" = "#D95F02",
                                "Neutral" = "#7097BB",
                                "Good" = "#1B9E77")) +
  labs(title = "Mean Loss Ratio by Driver Age and Bonus Score",
       x = "Driver age band", y = "Mean loss ratio",
       color = "Bonus score") +
  theme_minimal()








The U-shape across driver age holds within every bonus group, but the gap between bonus groups widens at the extremes. Young “Bad” bonus drivers are by far the most loss-making segment, while middle-aged “Good” drivers form the profitable core of the portfolio.


6.3.3 Correlation Heatmap of Numerical Variables

#Correlation between numeric variables (Spearman to handle skew)
num_vars <- clean %>%
  select(driver_age, vehicle_age, vehicle_value, power_to_weight_ratio,
         total_premium, total_incurred, total_claims,
         total_exposure, loss_ratio_w, frequency) %>%
  drop_na()

cor_mat <- cor(num_vars, method = "spearman")

ggcorrplot(cor_mat, type = "lower", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 3,
           colors = c("#D95F02", "white", "#1F4E79"),
           title = "Spearman Correlation Heatmap") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))








total_incurred correlates strongly with total_claims (≈ 0.95), confirming that the number of claims drives total losses more than any individual claim size in this portfolio. Premium and exposure are also strongly linked, as expected. None of the customer characteristics (driver age, vehicle age, vehicle value) shows a strong correlation with Loss Ratio individually — this reinforces the earlier finding that policy structure (type, bonus) explains more of the profitability variance than driver demographics.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
6.4 Temporal Dynamics of Profitability
The univariate temporal analysis in section 5.3 showed that the portfolio is growing rapidly. The question now is whether this growth is profitable. The four plots below track how Loss Ratio and frequency evolve across the three-year window, segmented by the risk factors identified above.

6.4.1 Overall Loss Ratio Trend

#Mean loss ratio by year — does the book get better or worse over time?
clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio_w)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_lr)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#D95F02", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_lr, 3)),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 4.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2022:2024) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Mean Loss Ratio by Year",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean loss ratio (Winsorised at p99)") +
  theme_minimal()








The mean Loss Ratio has risen consistently from 0.38 in 2022 to 0.46 in 2024 — a 22% relative increase in just two years. This is a material deterioration that warrants immediate attention.


6.4.2 Loss Ratio Trend by Policy Type

#Drilling into the deterioration by policy type
clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)) %>%
  group_by(year, policy_type) %>%
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio_w), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_lr,
             group = policy_type, color = policy_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2022:2024) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Mean Loss Ratio Trend by Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = break-even (LR = 1)",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean loss ratio", color = "Policy type") +
  theme_minimal()








The headline number conceals a much sharper story at the product level. COMP_N has crossed the break-even line in 2024, with a mean Loss Ratio of 1.01 — every euro of premium collected on this product is now being paid out in claims, before any expense allocation. TP doubled from 0.17 to 0.36 over the same period. CC and TPG are the most stable, with smaller upward drifts.


6.4.3 Claim Frequency Trend by Bonus Score

#Is the bonus signal still working over time?
clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(frequency)) %>%
  group_by(year, bonus_score) %>%
  summarise(mean_freq = mean(frequency), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_freq,
             group = bonus_score, color = bonus_score)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2022:2024) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Bad"     = "#D95F02",
                                "Neutral" = "#7097BB",
                                "Good"    = "#1B9E77")) +
  labs(title = "Claim Frequency Trend by Bonus Score",
       x = NULL, y = "Claims per policy-year", color = "Bonus") +
  theme_minimal()








The “Good” bonus group has stayed steady — its frequency barely moves from year to year. “Bad” bonus fluctuates more (sample is small, ~1,000 policies). The most concerning trend is Neutral: its frequency has risen from 0.45 to 0.62 between 2022 and 2024 — suggesting that some previously “average” customers are drifting toward the high-risk pool.


6.4.4 New Business vs Renewal Profitability

#Are new policies or renewals driving the deterioration?
clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w)) %>%
  group_by(year, business_type) %>%
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio_w), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_lr,
             group = business_type, fill = business_type)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_lr, 3)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2022:2024) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("New business" = "#7097BB",
                               "Portfolio"    = "#D95F02")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio: New Business vs Renewal",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean loss ratio", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Renewal policies (Portfolio) consistently underperform new business by 5–8 percentage points of Loss Ratio, and the gap is widening: in 2024, renewals hit a mean Loss Ratio of 0.51 vs 0.42 for new business. This is counter-intuitive — renewals should embody the company’s selective underwriting from prior years — and points to adverse selection in retention: the better customers shop around at renewal time, while the riskier customers stay.


6.4.5 Synthesis
Three independent signals — overall Loss Ratio drift, COMP_N crossing break-even, and renewal underperformance — all point to the same conclusion: the portfolio’s risk profile is deteriorating faster than the underwriting team is responding. This adds urgency to the business impact actions in section 8.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
8.1 Pricing and Product
Re-price or restructure COMP_N. With a mean Loss Ratio of 0.82 — roughly double the rest of the book — this product is the single largest profitability drain. A 15–20% rate increase, tighter excess structure, or repositioning to a different customer segment should be evaluated. Even a modest improvement here has portfolio-level impact because COMP_N still covers ≈ 16,000 policies.
Apply differentiated underwriting to the young Bad-bonus segment. Drivers aged ≤ 25 with a Bad bonus score are the worst sub-segment in the portfolio: they combine the U-shape age peak with the 2.3× higher claim frequency of Bad-bonus drivers. Tighter underwriting rules, mandatory excess, or simply declining the renewal of the most loss-making cohort can reduce tail exposure quickly.
Re-examine TP pricing. TP policies look profitable on average (mean LR ≈ 0.31) but have the highest coefficient of variation (5.19). This means the segment is exposed to severe third-party liability claims that the current premium may not adequately reflect. Reinsurance arrangements and excess-of-loss structures should be reviewed.
Address renewal adverse selection. The temporal analysis in section 6.4 shows that renewal policies have a mean Loss Ratio 8 percentage points higher than new business in 2024, and the gap is widening. This suggests the company is retaining a disproportionate share of its worst risks while losing better ones to competitors. Retention strategies should be risk-segmented — protect the good renewals with discounts or service perks, and let the worst ones lapse rather than offering across-the-board renewal discounts.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
8.2 Portfolio Management and Reporting
Track profitability and volatility as two separate KPIs. The analysis shows clearly that the most profitable segments are not always the most stable: Good-bonus drivers have the lowest mean LR but the highest CV; TP has the lowest mean LR but the highest CV. Management reporting that monitors only mean Loss Ratio will miss tail-risk build-up.
Interpret year-over-year trends with new-business mix in mind. Because ≈ 70% of policies each year are new business and the book grew 2.5× in three years, headline KPI movements are confounded by the changing mix. Mix-adjusted KPIs (e.g. Loss Ratio computed only on renewal policies, or stratified by year cohort) give a cleaner view of underlying performance.
Concentrate monitoring on the segments identified. Rather than tracking dozens of metrics across all dimensions, the underwriting committee can focus on five risk cells: (i) COMP_N policies overall, (ii) drivers ≤ 25 with Bad bonus, (iii) drivers ≥ 65 across all bonus levels, (iv) TP policies, and (v) policies with Loss Ratio > 2 in the prior year. These five cells capture most of the portfolio’s downside.

title: Take-home_Ex01
text:
8.3 Expected Financial Impact
If COMP_N alone were re-priced to reach a mean Loss Ratio of 0.55 (the portfolio average), the improvement would lift overall portfolio profitability by roughly 1.5 to 2.0 percentage points of Loss Ratio, equivalent to several million euros in annual underwriting result given the portfolio size. Combined with the young Bad-bonus underwriting tightening, total improvement could reach 3 percentage points without a single new product launch — making these the highest-ROI actions available to the underwriting team.
